content:
A list circulating on social media, titled "Before you convert to Islam", tells a would-be convert to follow a set of "roles" before pronouncing the testimony of faith. Its "major roles" include rejecting pork, never keeping a dog, fasting in summer heat "if you can cope", becoming a "zealot perfectionist", getting circumcised, removing any tattoo and avoiding people who have one, and rejecting gambling. It ends: "If these roles works for you then convert to Islam."

The list mixes real obligations with rules that no Muslim source contains, and it presents the whole as a test a person must pass before entering. This article aims to provide context to the first part of the list, insha'Allah, in seven answers: how a person enters Islam, what the religion asks about ease and effort, and what the sources say on food and drink, fasting and prayer, dogs, tattoos and circumcision. Two further articles take up what the list says about women and about apostates and LGBT friends.

The Quran sets the tone for every answer that follows: "Allah does not charge a soul except [with that within] its capacity" (2:286).[1]

The list makes its "roles" a condition to be met before the shahada. The Prophet (peace be upon him) taught the opposite order. When he sent Muʿādh ibn Jabal to Yemen, he told him to invite the people first to testify that there is no god but God and that he is God's Messenger, and only "if they obey you to do so", to teach them the five daily prayers, and after that the obligatory charity.[2]

The testimony is the door, and the practices are learned after it, one at a time. The five pillars on which Islam is built begin with that same testimony, followed by prayer, charity, the pilgrimage and the fast of Ramadan.[3]

A convert also enters with a clean record. When ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ hesitated to give his pledge until he was promised pardon for his past, the Prophet asked him: "Are you not aware of the fact that Islam wipes out all the previous (misdeeds)?"[4] The Quran says the same of those who cease their opposition: "what has previously occurred will be forgiven for them" (8:38).[1]

The list's sixth "role" tells the convert to become a "zealot perfectionist". The Prophet forbade exactly that. "Religion is very easy and whoever overburdens himself in his religion will not be able to continue in that way. So you should not be extremists, but try to be near to perfection".[5]

He gave the same instruction to those who teach others: "Facilitate things to people (concerning religious matters), and do not make it hard for them and give them good tidings and do not make them run away".[6] The Quran says of the religion it describes: "He has chosen you and has not placed upon you in the religion any difficulty" (22:78).[1]

When three men vowed to pray all night without sleeping, fast without a break and never marry, the Prophet rejected all three vows. He said that he himself fasted and broke his fast, slept, and married, and that "he who does not follow my tradition in religion, is not from me".[7] A convert who sets out to be a zealot is going against the Prophet's own teaching.

Some items on the list are real prohibitions, and we state them plainly. The Quran forbids "the flesh of swine" (2:173). It calls "intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone alters [to other than Allah], and divining arrows" a "defilement from the work of Satan" and commands believers to "avoid it" (5:90).[1]

The list omits the clause that follows the prohibition of pork in the Quran itself. "But whoever is forced [by necessity], neither desiring [it] nor transgressing [its limit], there is no sin upon him" (2:173).[1] The law of food is strict, and it is also bounded by need.

The list places alcohol among its "minor roles" and pork and gambling among the "major" ones. The Quran names intoxicants and gambling in the same verse (5:90), so a reader who wants to rank them has to rank them together.[1]

The list describes the fast of Ramadan accurately: food and drink are taken during the night, and the fast runs from dawn to sunset. It then adds "follow it if you can cope", as if that were a loophole.

The Quran writes the exemptions into the command itself. "So whoever among you is ill or on a journey [during them] - then an equal number of days [are to be made up]" (2:184), and the passage ends: "Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship" (2:185).[1] Those for whom fasting is a hardship beyond their strength are told to feed a poor person for each day instead (2:184).[1]

Prayer is "decreed upon the believers a decree of specified times" (4:103), five times a day.[3] The list calls this a "minor role" and adds "try to". A Muslim does try, and the same Quran that commands the prayer also tells him that God does not charge a soul beyond its capacity (2:286).[1]

The list says that keeping a dog inside the house is forbidden, "whether that's big or small dog". The sources draw a narrower line.

The Prophet said that angels do not enter a house in which there is a dog or a picture of a living creature.[8] He also said that whoever keeps a dog loses part of the reward of his good deeds each day, "unless the dog is used for guarding a farm or cattle", and other reports add hunting.[9]

So the sources discourage keeping a dog as a pet and permit dogs that work. The jurists also differed on the dog's purity. Ibn Rushd reports two views from Mālik, one that the leftover water of every animal is pure and one that excepts only the pig, while al-Shāfiʿī excepted both the pig and the dog.[10]

The same sources reward kindness to dogs. The Prophet told of a man who saw a dog eating mud from thirst, filled his shoe with water and gave it to drink, "So Allah approved of his deed and forgave him".[11] In the Prophet's own lifetime, Ibn ʿUmar reported, dogs used to pass through the mosque in Medina.[12]

A convert is asked not to keep a pet dog indoors. Nothing in the sources asks him to fear or mistreat one.

The Prophet cursed "the lady who tattoos (herself or others) and the one who gets herself tattooed".[13] Getting a tattoo is forbidden, and a Muslim does not get one.

A convert who already has a tattoo is in a different position. Al-Nawawī, commenting on this report, writes that a tattoo should be removed if it can be removed by treatment. If removal is possible only by wounding, and the person fears loss of life or limb or serious disfigurement, removal is not required, and "no sin remains upon him".[14]

He adds that the rule is the same for men and women.[14] Combined with the hadith that Islam wipes out what came before it, the convert has nothing to hide.[4]

The list goes further and tells the convert not to associate with people who have tattoos, or to be friends with them. No verse or report says so.

The Quran's rule for dealing with others, Muslim or not, is righteousness and justice toward those who do not fight you (60:8).[1] A tattoo on a friend's arm changes none of that.

The list says that a male convert "need[s] to be circumcised". The Prophet named circumcision first among five practices of the fitra, the natural disposition, along with trimming the moustache and clipping the nails.[15]

The schools of law disagreed about its status. Al-Nawawī reports that al-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad held it obligatory, while Mālik and Abū Ḥanīfa held it a sunna, a recommended practice.[16]

Even where it is obligatory, it is not a condition of becoming Muslim, and it gives way to harm. Al-Nawawī records that if a man is so frail that circumcision would put him at risk, it may not be done until his safety is likely, "because there is no worship in what leads to destruction".[16] A convert is a Muslim from the moment of his testimony, circumcised or not. Al-Nawawī also notes that even in his school circumcision becomes due only at maturity, and is recommended earlier because it is easier then.[16]

The bottom line

A person enters Islam by testifying that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is His Messenger. The Prophet taught the practices after that testimony, in stages, and he forbade the extremism the list recommends. The list is right that Islam forbids pork, intoxicants and gambling, and that it commands prayer and fasting, and it leaves out the exemptions the Quran writes into those same commands.

On dogs, the sources discourage a pet dog in the house and permit a working one, and they reward kindness to dogs. On tattoos, the rule is against getting one; an old tattoo is removed only where that can be done without serious harm, and no text tells a Muslim to shun tattooed friends. Circumcision of men is a practice of the fitra that the schools rank differently, and it waits where it would harm.

The list's closing line invites a person to convert only if every "role" suits him. The Quran's invitation is plainer: "There shall be no compulsion in [acceptance of] the religion. The right course has become clear from the wrong" (2:256).[1] God knows best.

Notes

  1. Quran 2:286; 8:38; 22:78; 2:173; 5:90; 2:184–185; 4:103; 60:8; 2:256, Saheeh International translation.
  2. Sahih al-Bukhari 1395 and 1458, report of Ibn ʿAbbās on the sending of Muʿādh to Yemen.
  3. Sahih al-Bukhari 8, report of Ibn ʿUmar, "Islam is based on (the following) five (principles)".
  4. Sahih Muslim 121, report of Ibn Shumāsa from ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ.
  5. Sahih al-Bukhari 39, report of Abū Hurayra.
  6. Sahih al-Bukhari 69, report of Anas ibn Mālik.
  7. Sahih al-Bukhari 5063, report of Anas ibn Mālik.
  8. Sahih al-Bukhari 3225, report of Abū Ṭalḥa.
  9. Sahih al-Bukhari 2322, report of Abū Hurayra; Sahih Muslim 1574 and 1575, reports of Ibn ʿUmar and Abū Hurayra, which add dogs kept for hunting.
  10. Ibn Rushd, Bidāyat al-mujtahid wa-nihāyat al-muqtaṣid (Cairo: Dār al-Ḥadīth, 2004), vol. 1, p. 34, Book of Purity, on the leftover water of animals.
  11. Sahih al-Bukhari 173, report of Abū Hurayra; compare Sahih al-Bukhari 3321.
  12. Sahih al-Bukhari 174, report of Ḥamza ibn ʿAbd Allāh from his father, Ibn ʿUmar.
  13. Sahih al-Bukhari 5940, report of Ibn ʿUmar; compare Sahih Muslim 2125, report of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd.
  14. Al-Nawawī, al-Minhāj fī sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim vol. 14, p. 106, on Sahih Muslim 2125, in the OpenITI text of the Shamela edition.
  15. Sahih al-Bukhari 5889 and 5891, report of Abū Hurayra.
  16. Al-Nawawī, al-Majmūʿ sharḥ al-Muhadhdhab, vol. 1, p. 300 (the positions of the schools), p. 302 (maturity) and p. 304 (the frail man) (Beirut: Dār al-Fikr), in the OpenITI text of the Shamela edition.
